perspective:
I am Sara Manuelito, a speech-language pathologist. Shirley Whiteplume is my long-time nurse colleague and close friend at our community health center.

- At the funeral of a patient we both knew, I saw Shirley looking somber and suspected she was deeply affected. I told her I knew it was hard and I saw how much she cared. Shirley said it had been tough and she kept thinking if there was something more we could have done. I said we did everything we could and should remember the good care and joy we brought him. She agreed but said it was hard to let go.
- During a coffee break, I raised our treatment decisions because I sensed she felt burdened. Shirley said she felt responsible and wondered if pushing for a different approach might have helped. I said we made the best decisions with the information we had and she shouldn’t carry the burden alone. She appreciated it but said it was hard to accept.
- After I observed Shirley being reserved and showing little emotion, I confronted her in our office. I told her I noticed she was holding back feelings and it was okay to be open. She said she didn’t want to seem unprofessional or weak. I said expressing emotions doesn’t make her weak and is healthy among friends. She said maybe I was right and she’d try to be more open.
- Later, because I felt my confrontation may have been too harsh, I apologized for coming on too strong. Shirley said it was a bit much but she knew I meant well and appreciated the apology. I said I was there for her however she needed. She thanked me and said talking helps.
- After some time, I noticed Shirley seemed to be doing better. I asked how she felt. She said she felt better thanks to our talks and my support. I offered to spend more time together outside work. She agreed and suggested planning something for the weekend.

I only know what I observed and what Shirley told me; I do not have direct access to her private thoughts beyond that.
